mappings.note: Attribution of inertia to Newton building on Galileo - the history clause of the first law's state-and-explain outcome. Same outcome as O11 and O43.
The 'State' half of LO-5 with no explanation or application demanded, so LO-5 alone and not the LO-64 or LO-65 pairings that the richer first-law items carry.
Despite naming the first law, the question asks specifically for zero net force implying zero acceleration, which is LO-64's content. Mapping the question and not the stem's label.
Produces a representation from a physical condition (C8.1) using constant velocity and zero net force (LO-64). No graph is supplied to analyse, so C8.1 rather than C2.1.
Recall of F = ma with no substitution - LO-6. LO-7 is reserved for producing a value from it.
Defines momentum. The frame has no momentum outcome; LO-6 is the nearest legal code because the answer frames momentum as the fuller form of the second law. Flagged as a poor fit.
Third member of the catching family; same outcome pair as O14 and O21, deliberately not split on wording.
Asks the student to supply one real-life application of extending collision time, which is squarely LO-65's 'apply Newton's laws to explain everyday life events', with the second law doing the work.
The SI-unit definition clause of LO-7, derived from F = ma as the stem requires.
Gravity-only content. C2.2 is the sole legal code touching it and has no outcomes beneath it. Duplicate of O39.
The 'State' half of LO-8 with no application - the outcome the chapter's own concept list is missing but the curriculum frame does carry.

The discriminating point is that the pair acts on two different bodies, which is what makes them ineligible to cancel on one free body (LO-62). Same pairing as O27, and what separates this from the bare statement in V85.

Reduced friction in a familiar situation. The third law is implicit in the answer but the question asks why walking is hard, i.e. about friction, so LO-63 leads. S119 explicitly demands 'interacting forces' and so earns LO-8 instead of LO-65.
Equal forces are the premise (LO-8); the asked reason is a = F/m (LO-6). Same shape as the apple-and-Earth pair.
Reaction propulsion in a real event - same pair as O31. Not LO-6: no acceleration or mass comparison is asked, only the direction of the reaction force.
Asks the student to supply an everyday example rather than analyse a given one, which puts LO-65 squarely on top of LO-8.

Defines the single-system idealisation: keep external forces, drop internal ones. LO-62 for deciding which forces count, C8.1 for the modelling move itself. The frame has no connected-systems outcome, so this is the nearest fit.
Restates the second law's two proportionalities as holding for a system's total mass. Symbolic, so LO-6; the systems framing has no outcome of its own.
Internal forces cancel because they are third-law pairs (LO-8) and the graded skill is choosing which forces enter the net force (LO-62). Same pair as O38.
Balance of weight against buoyancy (LO-62); the weight itself is the mass-times-g quantity that only C2.2 reaches. Buoyancy has no outcome in this frame.
Direct proportionality at fixed mass plus the same-direction clause. Qualitative, so LO-6.
Definition plus a worked example (LO-62) and then the consequence for the state of rest or uniform motion (LO-64). V70 stops at the definition, which is the split.
Two representations must be drawn (C8.1) and converted into a zero-net-force statement (LO-64). Drawing, not reading, so C8.1 rather than C2.1.
Unit of force plus the instrument that reads it. The measurement half has no outcome of its own, so LO-7's SI-unit clause carries the whole item. Flagged as a partial fit, like V68.
Addition then subtraction of forces with the direction of the resultant required. Same demand as V72, here inside a described scenario.
